newsitem.title: USA: First inflation-indexed muni sale goes 'very well'.
newsitem.headline: First inflation-indexed muni sale goes 'very well'.

text.p: Underwriters for the first sale of inflation-indexed tax-exempt municipal bonds said Thursday the Orlando, Fla., deal went "very well" and would likely prompt more issues of inflation-indexed munis.

"We've got a lot of interest. It's done very well," said Aaron Gurwitz, vice president and general manager for underwriter Goldman Sachs & Co. "It's a combination of retail and institutional. We had anticipated that it would be mostly of retail interest."

The deal involved $40 million of City of Orlando, Fla., water-sewer revenue refunding bonds. The bonds were issued out to 2015, but there is a mandatory tender in 2007, making them in effect 10-year bonds.
The deal featured fixed-rate serial bonds from 1997 to 2001. Coupons for later maturities were tied to increases in the Consumer Price Index, Gurwitz said.

For the 10-year bond the coupon was set at the CPI plus 125 basis points. If the CPI continued at 3.66. the annualized rate for February, the 10-year coupon would be 4.91. Coupons for comparable fixed-rate muni issues are currently about 5 percent.

"Of course if you buy a fixed rate bond, you are at risk if inflation increases. That's more of a risk than this. With this, if inflation increases, your income will come up to make up for some of the loss," Gurwitz said.
The city entered into an interest rate swap agreement with Goldman to hedge its risk, effectively taking it back to a standard floating-rate index, he said.
"They're substituting one form of floating rate for another," Gurwitz said.

The bonds were patterned after U.S. Treasury's Inflation-Indexed-Protection Series, or TIPS bonds, that the federal government began selling in January. Goldman said the Orlando issue is the first of its kind in the municipal market.

"As soon as the Treasury started talking about these things, we as bankers said, 'Hey, could we do this in the municipal market?' and we concluded pretty quickly it was feasible. We had to find an issuer to be the first," Gurzitz said.
Regulatory language from Internal Revenue Service already permitted such deals, he said.

Orlando Finance Director Mickey Miller, who has taken the city through some highly sophisticated deals in the past, "was clearly one of our first calls" when Goldman began shopping the idea, Gurwitz said.

Miller agreed to try the issue if it produced adequate savings. When all issuing costs are considered, the city's borrowing costs should be about 30 basis points below those for a traditional fixed-rate refunding, Gurwitz said.
"Generally speaking, the first few issuers who do it get the most benefit," he said.

He said Goldman Sachs was already in discussions with other municipalities that plan to issue CPI-indexed tax-free debt, but he declined to identify them. He predicted the deal would inspire similar deals by major issuers who have legal authorization to do the necessary hedges.
Currently, there are about $150 billion of variable-rate municipal bonds outstanding and "All of them are candidates," Gurqitz said.
"We're going to review the performance of this transaction next week. We're going to be looking at this very closely and so will our competitors," he said.
The bonds were rated A1 by Moody's Investor Service Inc and AA-minus by Standard & Poor's Corp, unchanged from previous Orlando water-sewer revenue bonds.
